title: Dean of LLM Tutors: Exploring Comprehensive and Automated Evaluation of LLM-generated Educational Feedback via LLM Feedback Evaluators
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to automatically assess the quality and safety of educational feedback generated by large language model (LLM) tutors before that feedback is shown to students. The authors argue that LLM-generated feedback can suffer from hallucinations, weak pedagogical quality, or poor alignment with assignment goals, which creates risks for learning quality and trust. To tackle this, they propose a “Dean of LLM Tutors” (DeanLLM) framework in which one LLM evaluates another LLM’s feedback and screens out low-quality responses.

The study introduces a comprehensive 16-dimension evaluation rubric covering feedback content, feedback effectiveness, and three hallucination types. Using university computer science assignment submissions, the authors created a human-labelled dataset of 200 synthetic student submissions and feedback generated by eight commercial LLMs. They then tested several LLMs as feedback evaluators using zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and fine-tuning. GPT-4.1 fine-tuned on plain-labelled examples achieved performance comparable to human coders for feedback evaluation.

The paper is situated in a higher education computer science context rather than K-12. The authors also used the best-performing evaluator to compare feedback quality across ten commercial LLM tutors on 2,000 feedback instances. They found that stronger reasoning models tended to perform better as evaluators, while some smaller models underperformed and GPT-4.1 nano produced more hallucinations. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can serve as scalable evaluators of LLM-generated educational feedback, but it is primarily a framework and benchmarking study rather than a student outcome trial.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed/archival-style empirical evaluation study with a clearly described labeling framework and model comparison, but it is not an RCT or QED on learner outcomes. The evidence is relevant and methodologically structured, yet it focuses on offline evaluation of model outputs rather than direct educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful operational benefits for scalable feedback moderation, but it does not report direct effects on student achievement, engagement, or teacher workload in authentic K-12 use. Its impact is therefore plausible but currently indirect and modest/unclear for educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated educational feedback evaluation and gating system ('DeanLLM') that screens assignment feedback before it is delivered to students, with hallucination detection and quality scoring across content and effectiveness dimensions.
Commercial LLM tutors generating feedback on university programming/computer science assignments (e.g., GPT-4.1, o3, o4-mini, Gemini, Deepseek) that are then evaluated for quality and hallucinations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that an LLM-based evaluator can automate feedback quality assessment at scale, reducing the need for human-only review of assignment feedback. In the main evaluation, fine-tuned GPT-4.1 reached human-expert-level performance (Accuracy 79.8%, F1 79.4%; human average Accuracy 78.3%, F1 82.6%) on the test set, indicating feasible automation for feedback screening (n=200 labeled feedback instances for evaluation; 2,000 feedback instances for deployment comparison).
finding.measure: Accuracy and F1 for feedback-quality classification; human-expert comparison; hallucination-detection accuracy
finding.study_size: n=200 labeled test feedback instances; 2,000 feedback instances compared across 10 LLM tutors

finding.finding_summary: The work does not measure student learning outcomes directly; instead, it evaluates the quality of feedback on university computer science assignments. The best evaluator (fine-tuned GPT-4.1) achieved human-level label accuracy, and Gemini 2.5 Pro produced the highest mean feedback-quality score (1.09) with 0 detected hallucinations across 200 feedback instances, while smaller models underperformed.
finding.measure: Feedback quality scores across 16 rubric dimensions; hallucination detection rates; evaluator accuracy/F1
finding.study_size: n=200 labeled feedback instances for evaluator training/testing; n=2,000 feedback instances for tutor comparison
